### Contributing guidelines

- [x] I have read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- [x] I have read [CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md](https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)
- [x] I have updated 'mini.nvim' to latest version of the `main` branch

### Module(s)

mini.files

### Neovim version

0.12.x

### Description

The mini.files help menu (`g?`) computes its own window width at [files.lua:2006](https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.files/blob/a249438d15fa6f64085ba83a9d1794d726aaf5ad/lua/mini/files.lua#L2006), but it doesn't take line numbers into account, should they be shown. As a result, long lines go slightly beyond the edge of the window (by 4 cells when there are 10 <= lines < 100, which I think is always true for the help window).

There's an easy fix (adding 4 to `config.width` on line 2012), but that's obviously not the right thing to do for general usage. One possibility I can think of would involve checking if `number`/`relativenumber` (I think these are the only two) are set and then conditionally adding `numberwidth` to `config.width`. It might be slightly more disciplined to actually compute the width of the number column by counting the number of digits in the largest line number. It looks like when `nonumber` and `relativenumber`, the width of the number column (though not actually `numberwidth`) is dynamically adjusted, so `numberwidth` may not be completely reliable.

If any contributors can opine on this, I'd be happy to make a PR.

### Reproduction

1. Create separate 'nvim-repro' config directory:
    - '~/.config/nvim-repro/' on Unix
    - '~/AppData/Local/nvim-repro/' on Windows

2. Inside 'nvim-repro' directory create a file named 'init.lua'.
   Populate it with the following content:

    ```lua
    -- Clone latest 'mini.nvim' (requires Git CLI installed)
    vim.cmd('echo "Installing `mini.nvim`" | redraw')
    local mini_path = vim.fn.stdpath('data') .. '/site/pack/deps/start/mini.nvim'
    local clone_cmd = { 'git', 'clone', '--depth=1', 'https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.nvim', mini_path }
    vim.fn.system(clone_cmd)
    vim.cmd('echo "`mini.nvim` is installed" | redraw')

    -- Make sure 'mini.nvim' is available
    vim.cmd('packadd mini.nvim')
    require('mini.deps').setup()

    -- Add extra setup steps needed to reproduce the behavior
    -- Use `MiniDeps.add('user/repo')` to install another plugin from GitHub
    ```

3. Run `NVIM_APPNAME=nvim-repro nvim` (i.e. execute `nvim` with `NVIM_APPNAME` environment variable set to "nvim-repro").
   Wait for all dependencies to install.

4. Replace this with description of interactive reproduction steps along with the behavior you observe.
   Feel free to include images/videos/etc, this helps a lot.

<details><summary>What to do after reporting an issue</summary>

After reporting the issue, it is safe (and even recommended for cleaner possible future bug reports) to remove 'nvim-repro' config from the system:
- Delete config directory ('~/.config/nvim-repro' on Unix).
- Delete data directory ('~/.local/share/nvim-repro' on Unix).
- Delete state directory ('~/.local/state/nvim-repro' on Unix).

</details>

comment_data.body:
Hello @thisisrandy,

Thanks for the issue!

I think that it is a bit too much to take user's window settings into account. 

Perhaps the following code is useful:

```lua

---@diagnostic disable: undefined-global

-- Define custom autocommand group and helper to create an autocommand.
local gr = vim.api.nvim_create_augroup('custom-minifiles', {})
local au = function(event, pattern, callback, desc)
  local opts = { group = gr, pattern = pattern, callback = callback, desc = desc }
  vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd(event, opts)
end

-- Override the built-in 'g?' keymap
local override_show_help = function(args)
  local nmap = function(lhs, rhs, desc)
    -- Use `nowait` to account for non-buffer mappings starting with `lhs`
    vim.keymap.set('n', lhs, rhs, { buffer = args.data.buf_id, nowait = true, silent = true, desc = desc })
  end

  nmap('g?', function()
    MiniFiles.show_help()
    vim.wo.number = true
    vim.cmd('wincmd 4>')
  end, 'Show Help')
end

require('mini.files').setup()
au('User', 'MiniFilesBufferCreate', override_show_help, 'Override show help')

```

Thanks for the suggestion!

I do agree with @abeldekat that this is a bit too much. Mostly because help window in 'mini.files' is always shown without line numbers (or any statuscolumn like elements). So if they are present, this means the user explicitly opted into using them. In fact, I am having trouble making line numbers show in the help window without some pretty general autocommands that would force this. Out of curiosity, @thisisrandy, how did you manage to show line numbers in a 'mini.files' help window?

As such, I think it is reasonable to also suggest users to adjust window with themselves if they choose to do so. Another way to do so (apart from the above comment) is something like this:

```lua
local adjust_minifiles_help = function()
  if vim.bo.filetype ~= 'minifiles-help' then return end

  -- Show line numbers
  vim.wo.number = true

  -- Adjust window width after setting line numbers
  local win_id = vim.api.nvim_get_current_win()
  local width = vim.api.nvim_win_get_width(win_id)
  local textoff = vim.fn.getwininfo(win_id)[1].textoff
  vim.api.nvim_win_set_width(win_id, width + textoff)
end
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('WinEnter', { callback = adjust_minifiles_help })
```

Maybe it can be a part of the other autocommand which shows line numbers in the help window in the first place.

Thanks to you both for the suggestions. I understand your concern. This is a "mini" repo, after all.

Also, apologies about the latter half of the issue (I pretty clearly didn't modify the Reproduction section)! I think I just straight up didn't scroll down after I typed up the description, which is a very weird lapse for me.

Anyhow, what's happening is that I have some autocmds set up to turn `cursorline` and `relativenumber` on and off depending on whether a given window is focused. I actually find it useful to have `relativenumber` on in `mini.files` windows (`<count>j/k` is ever useful), though maybe not so much in the help window, per se. I'm noticing now that it's on when I first open `mini.files`, gets blown away as soon as I start navigating the tree, and then turns back on with the same behavior after `g?` in the help window as well as the next non-help window after `q`. Given this, I might just use something like the guard in your autocmd to turn it off entirely when navigating the file tree.

The full extant code from my config follows:

```lua
local function augroup(name)
  return vim.api.nvim_create_augroup(name, { clear = true })
end

local cursor_line_only_in_active_window = augroup("CursorLineOnlyInActiveWindow")
-- TermLeave is specifically to fix lazygit integration. It massively screws up
-- when we e.g. switch from one terminal to another inside vim. I hardly ever
-- use the integrated terminal, and certainly never two at once, so this is
-- acceptable. Note that the integrated terminal also doesn't understand kitty
-- navigation shortcut commands, so it's kind of broken anyways
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd({ "VimEnter", "WinEnter", "BufWinEnter", "TermLeave" }, {
  group = cursor_line_only_in_active_window,
  callback = function(ev)
    if ev.file ~= "" and not string.find(ev.file, "^term://") then
      vim.opt_local.cursorline = true
      vim.opt_local.relativenumber = true
    end
  end,
})
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("WinLeave", {
  group = cursor_line_only_in_active_window,
  callback = function()
    vim.opt_local.cursorline = false
    vim.opt_local.relativenumber = false
  end,
})
```

I ended up adding the following to the top of the `WinEnter` etc. autocmd:

```lua
    if string.find(vim.bo.filetype, "minifiles") then
      vim.opt_local.number = false
      vim.opt_local.relativenumber = false
      return
    end
```
